article.title: Trump's Political Collapse
article.author: John Peeler
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Seldom has a party scored such a comprehensive demolition of its opposition. Yet the prime author was not the Democrats themselves, but their dominant adversary, Donald Trump. He created the economic conditions that impelled many of those who voted for him just two years ago to repudiate him now. His tariffs raised costs to consumers. His war in Iran led to the blockage of the Persian Gulf sea lanes and the explosion of fuel prices. His public obsession with self-glorifying monument construction, even as most people had trouble making ends meet, jut reinforced the public rage. He won’t acknowledge responsibility for this debacle, but he owns it. He can claim that Republicans lost because he wasn’t on the ballot, but every campaign rally just dug the hole deeper. Related: What I'll Be Watching Other Republicans bear some responsibility too. They cravenly prostrated themselves before him, rather than standing for the principles that had long defined their party. They deserved to lose, but their leader set them up. It was evident even before the polls started closing around the country that a wave was building. As Cooper took the North Carolina Senate seat, and Ossoff crushed his opponent in the Georgia Senate race, the battle shifted behind enemy lines. Surprisingly early in the night, South Carolina’s Senate seat fell into Democratic hands. New Hampshire, as expected, held Democratic. Then the evening got tense, but eventually almost all the tossup states fell to the Democrats, including Ohio, Iowa, Kansas(!) and Texas(!!). Eventually, the hotly contested Michigan seat fell to el-Sayed, and Susan Collins saw her thirty year Senate career brought to an end. At this writing, the outcome is unclear in Alaska and (wait for it!) In Mississippi! The Democrats will have at least 54 seats in the Senate, and maybe as high as 56. Similar results were happening in the House races; it was clear early that the Democrats would capture the majority. Now, with dozens of races still undecided, they will have at least 231 seats (majority is 218). I haven’t kept track of the state legislative races, but I think Democrats have gained substantially there too. In my former home of Pennsylvania, there is a good chance that the Democrats will win the Senate for the first time in decades. That would give them unified control of the state government. Related: Polls in the Hole? How Much Hope Has the GOP? As a new Massachusetts resident, I liked comparing the election in a solidly Democratic state with a solidly swing state like Pennsylvania. You can find pockets of relative Republican strength in Massachusetts, whereas most of the area of Pennsylvania is Republican. I used to live in a pocket of Democratic strength in a solidly Republican swath in the center of the state But even there, you can see change. Democrats did notably better than usual in that area, even though they still lost. In the state as a whole, Democratic Governor Shapiro was overwhelmingly reelected, and four Republican congressional seats were taken by the Democrats. Swing state politics is more exciting. What shall we make of this remarkable election? For one thing, the Republican Solid South has been irreparably broken. Coalitions of White moderates and liberals with minority voters won victories in both Carolinas, Georgia, and Texas, came close in Louisiana, and are too close to call in Mississippi. Related: Receivership: Agenda for a Democratic Congress Trump’s era has done incalculable damage to our democracy. We are now in the beginning of its end. The congressional Democrats must now investigate the many misdeeds, reassert control over finances, and establish a record of legislation (even if vetoed by Trump) that will show that they will address the ills that brought them victory. The election was not an endorsement of them: it was a repudiation of Trump and his priorities. The American people’s response to Trump over a decade is two-sided. Some bought into his appeal, and a good many still do. Most have stood against him, but have not fallen into the trap of violence. That is exactly what the Trump regime tried repeatedly to provoke; it would have led to authoritarian repression. We did not take that bait. And now he remains, for two more years, a pathetic shadow.
